lessonRef.subject: mathematics
lessonRef.unitTitle: Decision Analysis and Expected Value Capstone
lessonRef.title: Concept model A: expected payoff of a decision

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: Study both examples. The second one drops some of the wording of the first.

items.prompt: A has expected payoff $12, B has $9. Which, and what is ignored?

steps: A has the higher expected value.
Spread and risk tolerance are not captured.

items.prompt: Is a die with faces split 3/2/1 among three people fair?

sections.title: Guided practice
sections.directions: Work these with your teaching parent. Say the reason for each step out loud before you write it.

items.prompt: A game costs $14 to play. It pays $90 with probability 1/5 and nothing otherwise. Find the expected value to the player, and say whether the game is fair.
choices: $76; the game is favourable to the player
$-14; the game is unfavourable to the player
$4; the game is favourable to the player
$18; the game is favourable to the player

items.prompt: An insurer charges a premium of $14 and pays out $100 with probability 1/25. Find the insurer's expected profit per policy.
Option A has expected payoff $28 and Option B has expected payoff $9. On expected value alone, which should be chosen, and what does this criterion ignore?
choices: Option A; expected value already accounts for risk, so nothing is ignored.
Option B; expected value ignores the spread of outcomes and the decider's tolerance for risk.
Neither; expected value cannot compare two options.
Option A; expected value ignores the spread of outcomes and the decider's tolerance for risk.

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: Assess whether this is a fair decision mechanism: choosing between two people using a single fair coin flip.
choices: Fair; each person has probability 1/2, and the mechanism gives neither an advantage.
Fair, because any random device produces a fair decision.
Fair; each person receives probability 2/6 = 1/3, so the assignment is equal.
Not fair; the three probabilities are 3/6, 2/6, and 1/6, which are unequal.

items.prompt: A game costs $4 to play. It pays $30 with probability 1/10 and nothing otherwise. Find the expected value to the player, and say whether the game is fair.
choices: $-4; the game is unfavourable to the player
$-1; the game is unfavourable to the player
$26; the game is favourable to the player
$3; the game is favourable to the player

items.prompt: An insurer charges a premium of $13 and pays out $518 with probability 1/74. Find the insurer's expected profit per policy.
Option A has expected payoff $26 and Option B has expected payoff $9. On expected value alone, which should be chosen, and what does this criterion ignore?
choices: Option A; expected value already accounts for risk, so nothing is ignored.
Option A; expected value ignores the spread of outcomes and the decider's tolerance for risk.
Option B; expected value ignores the spread of outcomes and the decider's tolerance for risk.
Neither; expected value cannot compare two options.

sections.title: Mastery check
sections.directions: Mastery check. Work without help, then stop and hand this section in.

items.prompt: Assess whether this is a fair decision mechanism: choosing between three people by rolling a standard die, assigning faces 1–3, 4–5, and 6.
choices: Not fair; the three probabilities are 3/6, 2/6, and 1/6, which are unequal.
Fair, because any random device produces a fair decision.
Fair; each person has probability 1/2, and the mechanism gives neither an advantage.
Fair; each person receives probability 2/6 = 1/3, so the assignment is equal.

choices: $14; the game is favourable to the player
$58; the game is favourable to the player
$2; the game is favourable to the player
$-12; the game is unfavourable to the player
